name: Tomas Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I answer calls for a bank's card services line, so lost cards, blocked payments, people abroad whose card got declined at dinner. The centre's in a converted department store in town, and I'm on a team of twelve. I really like the fraud calls, because you're solving something real for someone who's panicking. What wears me out is the pay, honestly, and the way the queue never ends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do AI tools fit into that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use them all the time. The bank gave us an assistant that summarises the customer's last few calls, and I also use a free one on my phone at lunch to draft complaint replies, which I'm probably not supposed to do. I put my name down for the pilot team that tests the new chatbot, and I've already sent them a list of twenty things it gets wrong. My partner Dani thinks I'm mad for helping build my own replacement, and some days I agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, if I'm honest, because I was excited about some of it. Online I'd post that the tools were still useful even if they weren't magic. At work I'd tell people to keep learning them anyway, because a small edge is still an edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's safe in this one, which is good, but my money isn't any better. Dani and I rent a one-bed and we've got a few hundred saved, and that's after five years of working. A plateau keeps me employed, but it doesn't fix the low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on with the pilot team, because even a small tool needs people to test it, and it gets me noticed. I'd push for a pay grade for the people who train the bots, through the union rep, because right now we do it for nothing extra. And I'd start a little side thing, maybe setting up simple AI tools for small shops in town, for cash on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit flat. I'd be the guy at the bank's call centre who learned to drive a car nobody ended up buying, and I'd still think it was worth learning. The money worry is the same as always, sitting in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the union rep, rather than asking your manager directly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why the union rep, rather than asking your manager directly?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay you for AI help on weekends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I tried asking my manager, and she said it was development, which means unpaid. If one person asks, it's a favour. If the union asks for twelve of us, it's a job grade, and that's how it should be.

say: I'd say the AI hype was a **let-down** but the tools still help.
I'd tell colleagues to **keep learning** them anyway.
think: His **job is safe** but his pay is still low.
After five years he has only **a few hundred** saved.
do: Stay on the **chatbot pilot** team to get noticed.
Ask the union rep for a **pay grade** for bot trainers.
Set up **AI tools** for small local shops at weekends.
feel: Mostly **fine** but flat, with a steady **money worry**.

steps.text: Stay on the bank's chatbot pilot team and log its errors

Set up online booking for the local barber for a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when we let companies run the change on their own. At work I'd say we need a deal: retraining paid for, and people moved into new roles, not dropped. Online I'd be arguing with people who think it's either all great or all doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, half my floor is gone in this one, and I might not be in the half that stays. I'm average at the job, honestly, the main thing I've got is that I'm good with the tools. I'd rather be the person who teaches the bank's chatbot to say sorry properly than the person it replaces. The question is whether the bank needs ten of those or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask straight away to move from the pilot into the team that designs the chatbot conversations, even on a trial. I'd do an online course in conversation design in the evenings, the free ones first. I'd push the union for a retraining deal for everyone, and Dani and I would cut out the takeaways and try to save a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and sick at the same time. I'd love the new work, but if I don't get one of the few seats, I've got nothing to fall back on. There's one other call centre in town and it's doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bank might only need two people to train the bot. What if you're not one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said the bank might only need two people to train the bot. What if you're not one of them?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Dani feel about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take the AI skills somewhere else, maybe a council or a small company that needs someone to set things up. I'd have to look further than town, which means a longer commute or moving. I'd hate that, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a safety net right now, like an income for everyone while this settles. At work I'd say the union has to fight for every month of notice it can get. Online I'd be honest that I didn't see it coming this fast either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job ends in 2028, probably sooner, because it's pure thinking work. The bot-training role I wanted would go too, because AGI trains itself. Two years is enough time to learn something, but not enough time to save, and with a few hundred in the bank that's the part that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd squeeze every bit of AI work I can on the side, because small businesses will want help for a year or two before the AI just does it for them. I'd put all of that money away. Once it lands, I'd look for hands-on work in the gap before the robots, maybe installing equipment, maybe with Dani at the warehouse. And I'd be out with the union pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I'm usually the calm one about AI, so that's new. It's like being the one who brought the dog home and then it bites someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Dani's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens to Dani's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're very adaptable. Why doesn't that help more here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Warehouse work is hands-on, so Dani's got till 2031, roughly, which buys us three years. But the warehouse has already got robots for some of the shelving, so maybe less. We'd be living on one wage at some point, and that wage isn't big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set this up fairly, and we should start now. At work I'd push for a plan that moves agents into new roles. Online I'd share what I'm learning, because people need to see it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one gives me a real chance. Five years means I can try to jump from answering calls to building the thing that answers them, and still have a fallback if I fall. By 2031 the bot builds itself, but there's a few years where people like me are useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a proper part-time course in data or automation, something with a certificate, using any training fund the bank offers. I'd keep the weekend side work going and save all of it. I'd also start a basic qualification in electrical installation in year three, because hands-on work lasts till about 2034 here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but switched on. I'd have a lot of plates spinning. I'd worry about burning out more than about the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a lot for one person on lower pay. What gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a lot for one person on lower pay. What gives?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleep, and seeing friends. Dani would be annoyed with me most evenings. I'd try to keep Sundays free, but I wouldn't promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. At work I'd want a long-term plan for every agent, not just the keen ones. Online I'd probably be quite hopeful, which annoys people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be job-hunting by my mid-thirties, but I'd be choosing, not running. With ten years I'd stop thinking about my next job and start thinking about what kind of work I want my whole life to be about. Maybe something with people, maybe teaching others to use this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the bank job, because it's steady and the training fund's there. I'd do a proper qualification over two or three years, maybe in training or tech support. I'd build the side work slowly and save a bit each month, and I'd stay involved in the union so the bank pays for the change, not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a knot underneath. The knot is money: one bad year and we'd be in trouble even with ten years' warning. I'd still enjoy the learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of work would you want your life to be about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What kind of work would you want your life to be about?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helping people who are stuck, like the fraud calls, but in person. Maybe teaching adults to use technology, at a library or college. I like the moment someone gets it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to save and nowhere to go. What would help is a basic income while people retrain, and courses that are free for anyone who's lost their job to it. That would change everything for someone with a few hundred in the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets the money. The bosses will call the AI a cost saving, but every saving at a call centre is somebody's rent. I'd want that saving shared with the people who used to do the work.

headlineQuote: The bosses will call the AI a cost saving, but every saving at a call centre is somebody's rent.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old** bank card-services agent who uses AI tools every day.
He rents a one-bed with his partner Dani and has only **a few hundred** saved.
He volunteers on the **chatbot pilot** and wants to move into designing bots.
His mood moves from **uneasy** to alarmed when AGI arrives fast and leaves no time to save.
He mixes **adaptability** with strong union instincts about who gets the savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to save and nowhere to move.
whatWouldHelp: **Free courses** for anyone who lost a job to AI.
